reaction proceeding from the reactive form of the Michaelis complex (RE),
in which the hydroxyl group (OH3) forms a hydrogen bond with the catalytic base
Glu158. This configuration represents the starting point of the reaction, as the
interaction between the atom that performs the nucleophilic attack and the
catalytic base is essential for facilitating the attack.
To reach this state, the puckering of the carbohydrate was investigated through
unbiased metadynamics simulations (Figure S8), which revealed that OH3
initially forms a hydrogen bond with the pyrophosphate group. To establish a
suitable reactive conformation, the rotation of OH3 was examined to enable the
transition from the hydrogen bond with the pyrophosphate to that with the
catalytic base (Figure S10), a process associated with an energy cost of
approximately 2.5 kcal/mol. Once this hydrogen bond, required for the initiation
of the reaction, was established, a subsequent metadynamics analysis of the
carbohydrate puckering (Figure 5b in the manuscript) yielded the most
appropriate structure (RE) for launching the metadynamics simulation of the
reaction using the corresponding collective variables.
To clarify these processes, Figure S12 has been updated to depict the complete
catalytic cycle together with the associated energy profile.
6. The terminology “hidden intermediate” does not seem ideal. The designation
“transient species,” which the authors themselves use in parts of the text,
would be more appropriate and less ambiguous.
Response: we fully agree and we used “transient” in all places, including title
7. The use of the term “Minimum Energy Path” to describe a pathway on the free
energy surface (for example in Figure 6) is confusing. The authors should clarify
whether they computed a true minimum energy path on the potential energy
surface, or a minimum free energy path.
Response: We appreciate the clarification request. In our work, the path shown
in Fig. 6 is the minimum free-energy path (MFEP) on the metadynamics-
reconstructed free-energy surface (FES), expressed in the CV1–CV2 space for
fucose transfer, not a minimum-energy path on the potential energy surface. The
MFEP was obtained with MEPS and by following the lowest-free-energy route
connecting RE→TS→PR on the FES. To avoid confusion, we will (i) replace
“MEP” with “MFEP” throughout the manuscript, (ii) state explicitly in Methods and
in the Fig. 6 caption that the path is computed on the FES in CV space. These
wording adjustments do not affect the results or conclusions.
8. Finally, data accessibility is an issue. It was not possible to retrieve the
simulation data from the DOI provided
(https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.16733350) at the time of review. This must be
corrected to ensure transparency and reproducibility.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s observation. The simulation data are
now freely accessible for review and verification at the following DOI:
https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17558724.
In summary, the manuscript contains important results and has the potential to
make an important contribution to the field. Nevertheless, the issues outlined
above should be addressed through a careful revision before the paper can be
accepted.
Response: Thank you very much for your positive comments.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
This manuscript presents a comprehensive and multidisciplinary investigation
into the structure and catalytic mechanism of Arabidopsis thaliana FUT11, a core
α1,3-fucosyltransferase. The authors combine glycan microarray profiling, X-ray
crystallography, mutagenesis, cellular assays, and advanced computational
simulations to provide a detailed mechanistic picture of this plant-specific
glycosyltransferase. The work is well-executed and the findings are of broad
interest to the glycobiology community, particularly in understanding how
glycosyltransferases achieve substrate specificity and catalysis. However, major
and minor comments would need to be addressed to improve the quality of the
manuscript.
Response: Thank you very much for your positive comments.
Major comments:
1. While the MD simulations suggest that Glu158 induces conformational
distortion in the acceptor GlcNAc, the experimental electron density for this
GlcNAc is described as "partially defined". Additional experimental validation
(e.g., via NMR or alternative crystal forms) would strengthen this claim.
Response:
We performed NOESY and transferred-NOESY experiments on the glycan free
and bound to AtFUT11 across a range of mixing times. We did not observe
changes in NOE patterns between conditions, nor cross-peaks consistent with a
distinct populated ring pucker in the bound state. This is expected if the distorted
conformer is short-lived and interconverts rapidly with the chair, because NMR
reports ensemble-averaged observables; a minor state would only be visible if it
persisted on the millisecond timescale. We also attempted alternative
crystallization conditions but obtained the same lattice. Together, these data
neither prove nor refute a persistent distorted conformer. Accordingly, we have
tempered our language throughout to emphasize that our simulations are
compatible with, rather than conclusively demonstrating, enzyme-promoted
acceptor distortion, and we frame the mechanistic model as a plausible
asynchronous SN1/SN2-borderline pathway.
2. AtFUT11 exhibited low activity in catalyzing Lewisx synthesis in vitro. Is there
any potential physiological relevance of this activity? The authors should briefly
discuss about it.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the insightful comment regarding the low in
vitro activity of AtFUT11 in catalyzing Lewisx synthesis and its potential
physiological relevance. While AtFUT11 exhibits this activity in vitro, current
evidence indicates that this reaction likely does not have a significant
physiological role in Arabidopsis as it lacks the B4GALT1 gene and it does not
naturally produce N-glycans with terminal N-acetyllactosamine (LacNAc)
epitopes, which serve as substrates for Lewisx formation. Consequently, there
are no reports describing the presence of Lewisx epitopes in natural A. thaliana
N-glycans (doi:10.1074/mcp.RA117.000165). The observed activity appears to
reflect catalytic flexibility and enzyme promiscuity rather than a biologically
meaningful function. We have expanded this into the Results and Discussion
section to address this point with relevant literature references.
Minor comments:
Provide brief descriptive legends for Supplementary Movies 1 and 2 in the main
text or figure legends.
Response: We have moved the movies to the repository and we have included
the corresponding explanation for each Figure.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
This study is focused on a unique enzyme from the commonly studied plant
Arabidopsis thaliana. The enzyme is FUT11 which adds fucose residues in α1,3-
linkage to N-acetylglucosamine (GlcNAc) residues within the chitobiose core of
asparagine-linked (N-glycans) of the plants glycoproteins. The enzyme
represents a type of unique activity common in plants and many insects, but not
in vertebrates. The detailed catalytic mechanisms have not been defined for this
type of enzyme. Often glycans with this fucose linkage also have a xylose
residues in β1,2 linkage to mannose (Man) residues. Here the authors utilized a
recombinant enzyme, multiple glycan acceptors with or without xylose and other
extensions, a crystal structure of AtFUT11 bound to GDP and an N-glycan
precursor/acceptor (G0), unusual GT-B architecture for the enzyme, and
identified an asynchronous SN2-like mechanism for fucose addition that is
accompanied by distortion of the glycan structure to position the acceptor GlcNAc
for modification. Overall, the study is interesting and insightful about this unusual
type of fucosylation in plants and in other organisms. The key insights in this work
that may be of general interest is the evidence that the enzyme restructures or
distorts the acceptor for functioning, rather than passively binding, and provide
insights into novel catalytic strategies for glycosylating enzymes. While relatively
limited in scope with a focus on a single enzyme, this study is very well done, and
well presented, and represents a nice step ahead for understanding the catalytic
functions and activities of these novel core α1,3-fucosyltransferases.
Response: Thank you very much for your positive comments.
• It is not a massively critical issue, but having the recombinant enzyme would
allow kinetic studies beyond just the overall and relatively superficial screening
performed using microarrays. This could be insightful, as in that case the glycans
would be in solution and not immobilized on a surface. The authors should
provide some basic kinetic information for a few of the best acceptor substrates
and the GDP-Fuc donor (Km, Vmax) in their study to further enhance the
mechanistic insights. This type of information is useful in modeling within systems
biology approaches and predictive nature of glycosylation. I nature this enzyme
is competitive with many other enzymes.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion. In the revised
manuscript we now include steady-state kinetics for AtFUT11 with the GDP-Fuc
donor and the G0 acceptor, reporting 𝐾 , 𝑘 , and 𝑘 /𝐾 values obtained from
! "#$ "#$ !
nonlinear Michaelis–Menten fits (Supplementary Fig. 1b). These data
complement the microarray results, confirm hyperbolic behavior, and place
AtFUT11’s catalytic efficiency in a range comparable to benchmark mammalian
fucosyltransferases under matched donor/acceptor conditions. Unfortunately, we
are unable to provide data with other acceptors. We currently only have enough
materials to perform microarray-based analysis, which provides a miniaturized
assay, but not enough for solution-based measurements and the de novo
synthesis of these complex structures would require a significant synthetic effort.
• The differential activity of FUT11 on different acceptors in Fig. 1 might be related
to their unavailable or structural limitations because of the covalent attachment
to the glad slides.
Response: On glycan microarrays, only picomol amounts of the glycans are
immobilized in the individual spots and during the enzymatic reactions,
comparatively high excess of enzyme and donor concentrations (µM) are used.
Therefore, substrate accessibility, rather than catalytic turnover, primarily limits
the reaction rate. We always prepare glycan microarrays on Nexterion slide H
slides, that are coated with a 3D hydrogel that offers enhanced accessibility to
the immobilized carbohydrates, compared to other 2D based surfaces.
Additionally, our previous experimental results allow us to be confident that the
microarray-based enzymatic activity screening is a reliable technique perform a
substrate specificity screening. In our prior research, utilising FUT11 expressed
in Pichia pastoris (J Am Chem Soc 133, 16495–502 (2011)
https://doi.org/10.1021/ja205392z) with a smaller N-glycan microarray, we could
demonstrate a strong correlation between reactivity on the solid support and in
solution. Furthermore, FUT8 microarray-based screening published by us in Nat
Commun 11, 973 (2020). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-14794-z, was
completely correlated with the substrate specificity described in solution in a later
publication (Journal of Biological Chemistry, Volume 295, Issue 50, 17027 –
17045 DOI: 10.1074/jbc.RA120.014625).
• In earlier related studies on these types of enzymes in C. elegans, there was
evidence for such enzymes (CEFT1 and CEFT2) generating the core fucosylation
as well as the Lewis x antigen, using different types of acceptors, similar in
somewhat to what has been found here for A. thaliana FUT11. (DOI:
10.1093/glycob/cwm023).
Response: Thank you for this comment. The reviewer is correct regarding
CEFT1, as this enzyme indeed core-fucosylates using a different acceptor and,
in a very minor proportion, synthesizes the Lewis x antigen in C. elegans, similar
to what we observed for A. thaliana FUT11. However, CEFT2 does not core-
fucosylate according to the available literature—instead, it primarily fucosylates
LacdiNAc-containing structures and exhibits distinct specificity [Nguyen et al.,
Glycobiology, 2007, doi:10.1093/glycob/cwm023]. We have clarified this in the
Results and Discussion section and added an appropriate reference.
• The recombinant enzyme was expressed in mammalian cells, and the
glycosylation of the enzyme itself in such cells, might be abnormal compared to
the natural glycosylation in plants. There are several predicted sites of N-
glycosylation in FUT11/12, based on Supplementary Fig. 4Do the authors have
any evidence that ‘differential’ glycosylation might affect the outcome of their
experiments?
Response: We agree that recombinant expression in mammalian cells introduces
mammalian-type N-glycans on AtFUT11. To address whether this could bias our
results, we have mapped the three predicted N-glycosylation sequons present in
our construct (N337, N420, N481; Supplementary Fig.1) onto the AtFUT11
structure. All three sites are on solvent-exposed surfaces remote from the
donor/acceptor subsites and do not contact the loops that shape the active site.
Thus, while we cannot exclude generic effects on folding or stability, differential
N-glycosylation of the enzyme itself is unlikely to influence the fucosyltransferase
properties measured here (substrate recognition, turnover trends, or the
mechanistic features we report). We have noted this point in Results and
Discussion (“Substrate specificity of AtFUT11 revealed by glycan microarray
profiling”).
